Multilingual mediators in the shadows: a case study of a Japanese multinational corporation
contexts: In addition, Bartram et al. (2019) argued that Japanese MNCs are now adopting US-style HR policies and practices, such as performance-based pay and short-term employment, especially in their foreign subsidiaries.

Pudelko and Tenzer (2013), meanwhile, examine the differences in the extent to which expatriates exercise indirect control within foreign subsidiaries of Japanese, German and American MNCs, implying that bridge individuals in Japanese MNCs are engaged in enabling home-based practices rather more than those in German and American ones.

An iterative process of data analysis was undertaken involving concurrent collection of data and development of theoretical constructs regarding bridge individuals, while taking account of existing literature for Japanese MNCs (Miles & Huberman, 1994).

It is also evident that shadow organizational structures are likely in Japanese MNCs because Japanese MNCs have more substantial language barriers between subsidiaries and headquarters than do other Asian and Western MNCs. Connecting between subsidiaries and headquarters with multiple languages is also contingent on the nature of the MNCs’ businesses, as well as bridge individuals’ abilities.

Okamoto and Teo (2012) explored the bridging functions performed by Japanese PCNs acting as multilingual mediators in the Australian subsidiary of a Japanese MNC. Harzing et al. (2011, p. 284), meanwhile, defined mediators with bridging functions in German and Japanese MNCs as ‘bilingual individuals’ who ‘perform their bridging function as part of their normal job’, and then identify their main functions through terms such as linking pins, inpatriates and expatriates, non-native locals and parallel information networks.

Although JM has a long history and has operated for more than a hundred years since its incorporation in Japan, it is just one of many Japanese MNCs, and thus this case may neither represent nor be generalized to the population of Japanese MNCs.
That concerns the extent to which it can be generalizable, since it is a case study of three foreign subsidiaries in only a single Japanese MNCs.

Oki’s recent study of Japanese MNCs’ plants operating in Asia, however, highlights that individual country contexts still matter, even in Asian countries that appear superficially ‘like’ Japan (Oki, 2020).

The recent study by Oki (2020) concludes that Japanese MNCs have the most need of mediating functions, although whether Japanese PCNs play an important role in that mediation may be contingent on the extent to which the organization is oriented towards the host country’s market, and on the functional orientation of the MNC’s factories.
The first section reviews the existing literature regarding Japanese MNCs, HRM practices and bridge individuals.

The transfer of HRM practice in Japanese MNCs
Much of the literature examining the transfer of best practice from the headquarters of Japanese MNCs to their foreign subsidiaries has
approached the kind of bridging functions discussed above simply through quantitative analyses aimed at identifying the extent to which key management positions in the foreign subsidiaries of Japanese MNCs are filled by Japanese PCNs.
This need for a more complex articulation of expatriate bridging functions goes hand-in-hand with two recent trends in Japanese MNCs: Westernized practices and Management Localization.

There is some evidence for a shift to Western-style management practices in Japanese MNCs (Endo et al., 2015; Okabe, 2012; Sekiguchi et al., 2016), maybe in order to improve labour productivity (Aoki et al., 2014).

While all the studies discussed above applied quantitative approaches, Peltokorpi and Froese (2016) argued on the basis of qualitative analysis that the bridging function in respect to enabling home-country practices goes hand-in-hand with the ethnocentric staffing and home-based strategy pursued by many Japanese MNCs, as well as with the persistence of long-term oriented HR policies in these companies.

For Japanese MNCs, the institutional and cultural distance might be less still in Asian countries; as Iwashita (2016, 2019) demonstrates when revealing the full transfer of Japanese HRM practices in Thailand, a manufacturing hub in which many Japanese MNCs operate.
This may be especially true in the subsidiaries of Japanese MNCs, which tend to have a lower level of language skills, especially in English, than is the case in the subsidiaries of other MNCs.
